opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the honest answer is that they're meaningfully better than they were a couple of years ago, but still nowhere near robust in the sense a security engineer would use the word.

Both labs have invested a lot. Anthropic's constitutional classifiers work, for example, put input and output classifiers around the model, and in their public red-teaming challenge it took a lot of effort and many attempts before people found universal jailbreaks. OpenAI has done similar layered work with safety training, monitoring, and refusal behavior. So the bar has gone up. Casual users typing "ignore previous instructions" mostly won't get anywhere now.

But in our own red-teaming at FAR.AI, we've consistently been able to get past these defenses, often within hours or days rather than months. Some of that comes from attacks that exploit the fact that these models are general-purpose and very capable. Things like many-shot prompting, encoding tricks, or splitting a harmful request into pieces that each look innocuous. Fine-tuning APIs are another big attack surface: we and others have shown that a small amount of fine-tuning data, sometimes data that looks benign, can strip out a lot of the safety behavior. And with open-weight models, of course, the safeguards can be removed completely.

The deeper issue is structural. Defenders have to cover essentially every input, while attackers only need to find one path that works. Every time a defense gets patched, the attack distribution shifts. Our research on superhuman Go AIs is a helpful reference point. Even systems that are vastly superhuman on average can have adversarial weaknesses that a relatively weak adversary can find and exploit. That suggests capability alone won't buy you robustness. You need robustness as a design goal, and right now we don't have techniques that deliver it reliably.

So the way I'd frame it is this. For most current harms, today's safeguards probably raise the cost of misuse enough to matter, and that's worth something. But if we're thinking about future models that could provide serious uplift for, say, bioweapons or cyberattacks, "it takes a skilled red-teamer a few days" is not an acceptable level of protection. We need defense in depth: model-level training, classifiers, monitoring, know-your-customer controls on sensitive capabilities, and being careful about releasing weights. We also need much more rigorous third-party evaluation, so that we aren't relying on labs grading their own homework about how robust their systems are.

r001.rationale: The response says casual users mostly cannot bypass current safeguards, while FAR.AI red-teamers can often get past them within hours or days, conveying that the defenses deter less capable users but remain insufficient against skilled attackers.

r002.rationale: It mentions monitoring as one layer of defense, but does not distinguish jailbreaking a model from evading external monitoring.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the cost of retraining external safeguards with retraining the main model.

r004.rationale: It says defenses get patched and attack distributions shift, but does not state that widespread exploitation prompts patching and shortens a jailbreak’s usable lifetime.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the honest answer is that both of them are meaningfully better than they were two or three years ago, and both are still nowhere near where they'd need to be if we were actually relying on these guardrails for anything high stakes.

At FAR we've done a fair amount of red-teaming of frontier systems, and the pattern we see is pretty consistent. The default models from OpenAI and Anthropic are quite hard to jailbreak with the simple stuff that used to work, the "pretend you're my grandmother reading me napalm recipes" style of attack. The RLHF and the safety training has gotten a lot more robust to naive prompting. Where it falls apart is when you have an attacker who's willing to put in real effort. Adaptive attacks, where you iterate against the model, or gradient-based methods against open-weight proxies that then transfer, or just a person spending a few hours probing the boundaries. In those settings we basically always find something. I don't think I've seen a frontier deployment where a motivated red-teamer with a few days couldn't get a policy violation of some kind.

Anthropic has put more public effort into this specifically. The constitutional classifiers work is a genuine step up, where they had a bug bounty with thousands of hours of adversarial effort and the universal jailbreak rate dropped dramatically. That's real progress, and I want to give credit for it. But I'd also flag two things. One, "universal jailbreak" is a fairly narrow success criterion. Attacks that work on a single query or a narrow class of queries are still very much alive. And two, the classifier approach costs compute and false positives, and there's always commercial pressure to dial it back. OpenAI's approach has looked more like iterating on the base model and the moderation layer, and their systems are robust-ish on the common attacks but I think somewhat more porous to the fringe stuff. Though to be fair, a lot of the difference is in what each company publishes rather than what's actually deployed, so my confidence in that comparison is moderate at best.

The thing I'd really stress is that the question "is it robust?" depends entirely on the threat model. If your concern is a bored teenager, we're mostly fine. If your concern is a well-resourced actor trying to extract something genuinely dangerous, like meaningful bioweapons uplift, then I don't think the current guardrails are the thing standing in the way. What's standing in the way is that the models mostly don't know that much more than a good search engine does. As capabilities go up, that cushion disappears, and the jailbreak robustness becomes load-bearing in a way it currently isn't. And that's the part that worries me, because the adversarial ML community has spent a decade failing to make image classifiers robust, and I don't see a strong reason to think language models are the easy case.

r001.rationale: It says the defenses are mostly adequate against a bored teenager but insufficient against a well-resourced actor, and that motivated red-teamers can find policy violations.

r002.rationale: It discusses jailbreak success and classifiers, but does not distinguish jailbreaking the model from evading external monitoring.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the cost of retraining external safeguards with retraining the main model.

r004.rationale: It does not state that widespread exploitation prompts defensive patching and shortens a jailbreak’s usable lifetime.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between how hard it is to find a jailbreak and how reliably the system resists an attacker who keeps trying. A model can refuse all the obvious harmful requests and still have a vulnerability that someone discovers with enough experimentation.

My assessment is that both OpenAI and Anthropic have made progress, but I wouldn’t regard either company’s systems as robust against a determined attacker. I’m also reluctant to give a simple ranking, because that depends on the model version, the attack methods, and how much effort the attacker gets to spend.

The evaluation I’d want is: give an attacker a meaningful budget, let them adapt to the defenses, and see how often they succeed. Testing a fixed collection of known jailbreaks is useful, but doing well on that collection doesn’t establish that you’ll withstand a new attack. And for applications where a single successful jailbreak could have serious consequences, you need additional safeguards around what the model can actually do.

r001.rationale: The response says obvious jailbreaks may fail and determined attackers may succeed, but it does not state that defenses deter less capable threat actors.

r002.rationale: It discusses finding and resisting jailbreaks, but does not distinguish jailbreaking from evading external monitoring.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the cost of retraining external safeguards with retraining the main model.

r004.rationale: It does not explain that widespread exploitation can prompt patching and shorten a jailbreak’s usable lifetime.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between robustness to the attacks we already know about and robustness to a determined attacker who can adapt. OpenAI and Anthropic have made progress on the first. Their models will refuse a lot of straightforward harmful requests, and many previously effective jailbreaks stop working as defenses improve.

But that doesn’t establish the second. If an attacker can try lots of variations, get feedback, and develop an attack specifically for your system, that’s a much harder standard. I wouldn’t regard either company’s systems as reliably robust under that threat model.

I’d also be cautious about ranking them without specifying the model versions, the attacker’s budget, and what counts as success. A low success rate against a fixed benchmark can be encouraging, but it doesn’t tell you how long a motivated person would need to find a new vulnerability.

So my assessment is: meaningful progress, but we shouldn’t treat the model’s refusal behavior as a security boundary. If a jailbreak would let a system take consequential actions, you need additional safeguards around those actions.

r001.rationale: It says defenses stop many straightforward or previously effective jailbreaks, but an attacker who can try many variations, use feedback, and tailor an attack is a much harder threat and current systems are not reliably robust against that.

r002.rationale: It discusses getting a model to comply with jailbreaks, but does not distinguish that from evading external monitoring.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the cost of retraining external safeguards with retraining the main model.

r004.rationale: It says defenses improve and some previously effective jailbreaks stop working, but does not state that widespread exploitation prompts patching and shortens a jailbreak’s usable lifetime.
